title: A lab photograph is evidence of existence, not of a result: what the flame, the balance and the chromatograph can and cannot show
summary: Three photographs from the experimental campaign: a producer-gas flame, a laboratory balance and a gas chromatograph. Each stands for one link in the measurement chain (what the rig made, how fuel and samples were weighed, how the gas was analysed). Read them for what they document, and for what the numbers that come from them need in addition.

media.alt: Photograph looking up into a black, sooty conical burner hood with a bluff central body. An orange, swirling flame fills the ring between the central body and the hood, with a pale grey-white region in the middle and a corrugated metal roof visible behind.

source.caption: Producer-gas flame from the rig
source.note: Group explainer for the three experiment photographs. Figure 08 is captioned as the downdraft gasifier rig, but the image shows a laboratory analytical balance with a crucible (see 'As drawn'); the explainer follows what the image shows.

read_the_figure.question: What does each photograph show about how the data were produced, and what more would be needed before it counts as evidence for a number?
read_the_figure.axes: No axes and no scale in any of the three photographs. The flame photo is a frame from video taken from below; the balance photo is a close-up of the instrument and its display; the chromatograph photo is a wide shot of a bench.
look_at: Flame (07): a ring of orange, swirling flame around a central body inside a blackened hood. The centre is pale and hazy. Orange suggests soot or particles; a clean hydrogen or carbon-monoxide flame is much paler. The black coating on the hood is deposit.

Balance (08): an Ohaus Adventurer analytical balance with a glass draught shield and a white crucible on the pan. The display reads 50760 mg, that is 50.760 g. A calibration sticker below the display carries a date range that looks like 09-02-2018 to 08-02-2019 (handwritten, hard to read); the file name suggests the photograph was taken on 10 May 2018.

Chromatograph (09): a gas chromatograph (the beige box with a small display, at the right) with a PC and monitor for data acquisition, and a wall panel of pressure regulators with gauges above the bench for the supply gases.
The links in order: fuel and ash are weighed, gas is made and burned or sampled, the sample is injected into the chromatograph, the PC integrates peaks.
read_the_figure.proves: That the experiments were done with physical equipment: a flame was produced, a calibrated balance was used and a chromatograph with its gas supply was in the lab. They show the measurement chain, not a measured value.
if_wrong: A photo used as if it were a result: a burning flame does not tell the composition, the heating value or the efficiency.
A caption that says one thing while the image shows another (see below) weakens trust in the others.
A flame colour read as a composition measurement: colour depends on soot, temperature and air supply as well as on the gas.
must_check: Date, run identifier and operating condition are stated for each photograph.
Calibration status of the instrument (the balance sticker is legible only partly).
Which detector, column and carrier gas the chromatograph used, and which calibration gas; the photograph shows none.
A scale or a reference object, if size matters.
as_drawn: Figure 08 is captioned 'Downdraft gasifier rig, campaign run' (525 mm ID, 2.165 m tall, May 2018), but the image is a laboratory balance with a crucible. The numbers in the caption (525 mm, 2.165 m) cannot be checked against the photograph. The owner should confirm that the right image has been used.
Balance reading: 50760 mg is 50.760 g. A resolution of 1 mg on 50.760 g is a relative reading resolution of 1 / 50760 = 2 x 10^-5.

A typical air-blown producer gas is about half N2 by volume. The measured composition of the gas in the parity figure adds to about 47 to 50 vol% for H2, CO, CO2 and CH4; the remainder is N2, which the chromatograph also reports according to the caption of figure 09.

terms.meaning: The combustible gas made in a gasifier, mainly H2, CO, CH4, CO2 and N2 when air is used.
A fixed-bed reactor in which fuel moves down and gas leaves at the bottom, passing through the hot combustion zone, which cracks the tars.
A balance reading to a milligram or better, protected from draughts by a glass shield.
Separation of a gas mixture on a column, so that each species reaches a detector at its own retention time; the peak area is proportional to the amount.
The detector's peak area per unit of a species, found by running a calibration gas of known composition.
How long a species takes to elute from the column; it identifies the species.
Comparing an instrument against a reference standard and recording the correction, with a date.
Heat released by burning one unit of gas completely, with water leaving as vapour.

remember: A photograph documents a measurement chain; it never replaces the number.
A chromatogram needs a calibration to become a composition.
Compositions on a dry basis must add to 100 percent, N2 included.

understand.title: Why the three belong together
understand.text: The flame shows that combustible gas was made. The chromatograph turns a gas sample into composition. The balance gives the masses that go into the mass balance. Remove any one of the three and a number in the results chain cannot be defended.

understand.title: What a flame can tell you qualitatively
understand.text: Orange, luminous flame means incandescent particles, often soot or tar. A clean mixture of H2 and CO burns with a faint pale flame. The flame in the photograph is orange with a black deposit on the hood, which suggests that some particulate or tar was in the gas or that the hood is the source of the glow. It is a hint, not a measurement.

understand.title: What the balance contributes
understand.text: Fuel, char and ash masses enter the closure of the previous explainer. A balance reading with 1 mg resolution on tens of grams is good to about 2 parts in 100,000; the real uncertainty is in sampling and moisture, not in the balance.

steps.title: From peak area to mole fraction
steps.note: Each peak area A_i is divided by its response factor from calibration; normalising over all species gives the mole (and, for ideal gases, volume) fraction. This is the generic chromatography calculation.

steps.title: Dry composition adds to one
steps.note: If the sum of the raw values is far from 100 percent, a species is missing or the calibration is off. This is a free check.

steps.title: Mixture heating value
steps.note: Only combustible species count. The coefficients are standard lower heating values per normal cubic metre. This is what the flame carries and what cold-gas efficiency starts from.

steps.title: Relative resolution of a reading
steps.note: Smallest resolvable step as a fraction of the reading. It is the reading resolution only, not the total uncertainty.

worked.title: Heating value of a producer gas
worked.problem: A dry producer gas has 25 vol% H2, 9 vol% CO, 1.5 vol% CH4 (illustrative values of the size seen in the project's parity figure). What is its lower heating value, and what is the sum of the combustibles?

solution.text: Weight each species by its standard LHV.

worked.answer: About 4.4 MJ per normal cubic metre, from 35.5 vol% combustibles; the rest (CO2 and N2) does not burn. The composition is illustrative, not a measured run.

analyze.q: The flame in the photograph is orange. List two things that would make a gasifier flame orange and one measurement that would tell them apart.
analyze.hint: Soot or tar, sodium contamination, and a second flame colour check with a camera filter or a tar sample.

analyze.q: The caption of figure 08 says it is the gasifier rig; the image shows a balance. What could have happened, and what would you do?
analyze.hint: A wrong file or a wrong caption; ask the owner for the original photograph.

analyze.q: Why does a chromatograph need a calibration gas of known composition?
analyze.hint: Peak area is not equal to amount for different species.

evaluate.q: Do these photographs add credibility to the numerical results? Which would you remove and why?
evaluate.hint: Evidence of a chain versus decoration.

evaluate.q: A reader sees a bright orange flame and concludes that the gas is rich in hydrogen. How would you correct the conclusion?
evaluate.hint: Flame colour is dominated by soot and particles.

create: Write a one-line caption for each photograph that says what it shows, the date and where the corresponding data appear in the project.
Design a calibration check for the chromatograph before each run: which gas, how many injections, and what tolerance you would accept.

checks.q: What is a chromatograph's output and how does it become a composition?
checks.answer: A set of peaks at retention times identifying species; each area is divided by the species' response factor and the results normalised to give fractions.

checks.q: A balance reads 50760 mg with a 1 mg resolution. What is the relative resolution?
Measured H2, CO, CO2 and CH4 add to about 48 vol%. Where is the rest?
checks.answer: Mostly nitrogen from the air used in gasification, which the chromatograph also reports.

checks.q: What does an orange flame prove about the gas composition?
checks.answer: Almost nothing quantitative: luminous orange means incandescent particles such as soot, not a particular H2 or CO fraction.

checks.q: How would you make the flame photograph into evidence?
checks.answer: Add the run identifier, SBR and ER, the date and the corresponding gas analysis next to it, and a scale or reference object.
